content:
Never ever do something you can’t afford financially or emotionally. 

That being said, some make emotional decisions over the idea of “free work.” 
As they say, “nothing in life is free.” 

People treat this as a privilege issue but I think it’s an opportunity issue. Many can afford it but aren’t taking the risk because they don’t value the exposure, relationships, learnings and I respect that if that’s one’s opinion. 

Obviously sustained free work is impossible and the length is predicated not only on one’s savings but also their side hustle, how they spend their money to live, if they’ve made money before, if they have to help their parents, or a number of other things. 

An increasing amount of skills that are wanted in the real world don’t require a college degree, nor has the curriculum caught up to the actual needs of the marketplace. 

And for many, the opportunity to work closely with others who have succeeded in the industries that they are most interested in, or even better – and this is really where I’m going with this hypothesis – if you’re able to get to the top 100 people in your desired craft or industry and that requires an unpaid free consultation, an unpaid 2 month internship, a 4-month project, or 2 videos to be made for that person, then this is something you have to highly debate. 

This is “your foot in the door.”

content:
The term "toxic positivity" fascinates me. 

The concept that there is even an ability to be “toxically positive” is a misunderstanding of “positive.” What people are really trying to say is “delusion.” Instead of weaponizing the term, stop saying “toxic positivity” and start saying delusional, which is what it really means.

For me, all I talk about is practical truths. All I believe in is accountability. The market is always right. But I also believe life is how you see it. I believe if you wake up and everyone you care about is healthy, it’s a great day. Optimism is defined as the “hopefulness and confidence about the future or the successful outcome of something.”

I think that’s practical. You can be optimistic while acknowledging where there’s adversity, or while having compassion for yourself when you’re having an off day. Optimism is about being thrilled about your next at-bat, while acknowledging you’re not guaranteed to hit a home run. Whereas delusion sits, to me, like you just sit on your couch, hold your breath, cross your fingers, and hope it’s going to be okay with no action.

It’s sad to me that people confuse positivity with delusion. There’s a reason two different words exist.

content:
Your plans won't save you.

(But your preparation will.)

I used to obsess over the perfect plan.

Every step mapped out. Every variable accounted for. A clean, beautiful path from A to B.

Then life happened.

Here's what I've learned:

Planning is based on the expectation of order.

Preparation is based on the expectation of chaos.

One assumes the world will cooperate with your timeline.

The other assumes it won't.

The person with the perfect plan falls apart the moment something goes sideways.

The person who prepared never needed things to go right in the first place.

Plan for order and you'll be destroyed by chaos.

Prepare for chaos and you'll thrive in any condition.

The most resilient people I know aren't better planners.

They're better preparers.

They build skills instead of spreadsheets.
They train responses instead of scripting outcomes.
They invest in adaptability instead of certainty.

Stop perfecting the plan.

Start preparing for everything the plan can't predict.

content:
Your brain literally shrinks mountains.

(But only when you're not alone.)

In a ​2008 paper​ published in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, researchers at the University of Virginia sought to study the impact of social support on how we perceive challenges.

In the first study, the researchers had a group of participants stand at the base of a steep 26° hill wearing a heavy backpack. Some of the participants were alone, while others were paired with a friend. Then they asked the participants to estimate the hill's steepness.

The findings were fascinating:

1. Participants who were paired with a friend estimated the hill to be significantly less steep than those who were alone.
2. Relationship duration with the friend correlated negatively with perceived steepness. The longer the friendship, the gentler the hill appeared.

The researchers concluded that the brain treats supportive relationships as a psychological energy resource. When you feel connected, your brain effectively lightens the load.

The challenge doesn't change, but the perception of that challenge does.

It's called The Social Slope Effect.

So, how do you take on life's most challenging mountains?

With a friend.

Because challenges and struggles are inevitable.

But facing them alone is optional.
